title: The Hardest Part of a Real Estate Developer's Pitch Deck: the Financial Plan
seoTitle: The Hardest Slide in a Developer's Pitch Deck
description: For real estate developers, the financial plan is the hardest slide in the pitch deck. What it must answer, and the one rule that makes it credible.
answer: The financial plan is the hardest slide in a developer's pitch deck. It must answer what each unit will sell for, what it will really cost to deliver, and how much overhead the company will carry, then show investors a return. The only rule: be honest with yourself first.
body:
If you are a real estate developer raising money for a project, one slide in your pitch deck will take more work than all the others together: the financial plan.

## Three questions you must answer

1. **What will each unit sell for?** Not an average price per square foot for the building, but a realistic price for each unit based on its floor, view, size and the market around it.
2. **What will it cost to deliver those units?** Land, design, permits, construction, financing, marketing and sales commissions, with a contingency for what you cannot predict.
3. **How much overhead will you carry?** Once your organization is set up, with your team, offices and everything else, those costs run every month until the last unit closes.

## Then make it interesting for investors

Investors put money into your project because they need to make money from it. Your numbers have to show a return that justifies their risk and the time their capital is locked in.

## The only rule: be honest

The temptation is to push the sale prices up and the costs down until the return looks attractive. Investors have seen that many times, and they discount it. Worse, you start believing your own spreadsheet.

Be very honest, first with yourself and then with your investors. A plan that holds up under questions is worth more than a plan that looks spectacular on one slide.
takeaways: The financial plan is the hardest and most scrutinized slide in a developer's deck.
It must cover unit-by-unit sale prices, real delivery costs and ongoing overhead.
Investors need to see a return that justifies their risk and time.
Honest numbers build more credibility than optimistic ones.
faq: What goes into a real estate development financial plan?
Projected sale price of each unit, total development costs including land, construction, soft costs and financing, company overhead, timeline, and the expected return for investors.
Why do investors discount developer projections?
Because many projections are optimistic. Conservative, well-supported numbers make a developer more credible.
How do I price each unit in a presale project?
Start from comparable sales nearby, then adjust each unit for floor, view, orientation, size and layout.
